metadata.title: Graph Traversal: BFS Queue vs DFS Stack
metadata.subject: Computer Science
metadata.objective: Show BFS/DFS visiting order and frontier differences.
misconceptions: DFS always finds the shortest path in an unweighted graph
Visited nodes can be revisited forever
expectedUnderstanding: BFS's FIFO queue processes nodes in nondecreasing unweighted distance from the source.
DFS's LIFO stack follows one branch deeply, so its visit order is not a distance order.
A discovered/visited check marks a node once, so later encounters are skipped and traversal terminates.
On this graph BFS reaches E in two edges, while DFS reaches E at depth three.

primitives.text: Start at A. Queue front is left; stack top is left. BFS is FIFO; DFS is LIFO.

checkpoints.title: Frontier, not visited
checkpoints.body: After A, the queue holds B and C. They are discovered, not yet visited. The visited set contains only A; queue order is FIFO with the front on the left.

checkpoints.title: BFS moves in layers
checkpoints.body: B and C are at distance 1; D and E are at distance 2. BFS will finish both distance-1 nodes before either distance-2 node, so its order is not alphabetical luck.

checkpoints.title: BFS distance guarantee
checkpoints.body: BFS is done: A0, B1, C1, D2, E2. The shortest A-to-E path is A-C-E, two edges. On an unweighted graph, first discovery by BFS is a shortest path.

checkpoints.title: Predict DFS
checkpoints.body: DFS just popped B and pushed D, so D is on top of the stack while C waits below. Which node will DFS process next, C or D? Answer before continuing.

checkpoints.title: DFS is not shortest-path order
checkpoints.body: DFS reached E at depth 3 along A-B-D-E. BFS reached E at distance 2 along A-C-E. DFS followed the deep branch first, so its visit order cannot be read as distance order.

checkpoints.title: Same graph, different orders
checkpoints.body: Final orders: BFS A,B,C,D,E; DFS A,B,D,E,C. In each traversal, every node entered the frontier once and was visited once; checks skip repeats. DFS is useful for deep exploration, not for shortest unweighted paths.

narration.text: Both traversals start at A, but BFS uses a queue and DFS uses a stack.
BFS has discovered B and C at distance 1; D is next in the queue at distance 2.
C gives E distance 2, so BFS already has the shortest A-to-E path.
DFS resets at A and pushes C then B, so B is on top of the stack.
DFS goes B to D and reaches E at depth 3, while C still waits.
DFS finally visits C last, so its order is A, B, D, E, C.
Both visit every node once, but only BFS's order follows distance layers.

fallback.text: BFS and DFS both start at A. BFS uses a FIFO queue, so nodes leave in discovery order. From A it enqueues B and C at distance 1. It processes B, which enqueues D at distance 2; next it processes C, which enqueues E at distance 2; then D and E. BFS order is A, B, C, D, E and distances are A0, B1, C1, D2, E2. Thus the shortest A-to-E path is A-C-E, two edges. DFS uses a LIFO stack. After A it pushes C then B, so B is on top. B pushes D, and D pushes E. DFS therefore reaches E at depth 3 along A-B-D-E before returning to C. DFS order is A, B, D, E, C. C is only one edge from A but is visited last. This shows that DFS does not guarantee shortest unweighted paths, even though every node is visited exactly once. A visited set records a node when it is processed, and a discovered check prevents it from being pushed twice, so traversal terminates.

accessibility.alt: Graph: A connects to B and C; B to D; C to E; D to E. BFS order A,B,C,D,E with E at distance 2 via C; DFS order A,B,D,E,C reaches E at depth 3. Labels show depth and visited marks.
